Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:36: Moreover, even one who has begun studying and boasts of it, saying that he is a Torah scholar, his punishment is great, as we say in tractate Bava Batra (98a): Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav, whoever is proud of the cloak of a Torah scholar without being a Torah scholar is not admitted into the presence of the Holy One, blessed be He — here it is written (Habakkuk 2:5), "an arrogant man is not at home [yinveh]" and there it is written (Exodus 15:13), "to Your holy home [neveh]." Thus far his words. It seems to me that this is measure for measure: just as he drove the Shechinah from his house [by his arrogance], so, when his soul ascends above, it will be driven from the presence of the Holy One, blessed be He, for the Shechinah dwells only in a broken heart — this is what is said in Tikkunim (22b), that one must make a fitting dwelling for it in his heart, meaning that he be lowly and not angry, for once he is proud, the Shechinah flees from him, since he installs the maidservant in the place of her mistress; therefore "he is not at home," just as there was no home for the Holy One, blessed be He, in him, so there will be no home for his soul in the World to Come.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:37: Among the things that delay the redemption is haughtiness of spirit, as is said in Sanhedrin (98a): Ze'iri said in the name of Rabbi Chanina, the son of David will not come until the haughty-spirited cease from Israel, as it is said (Zephaniah 3:11), "for then I will remove from your midst those who exult in your pride, and you shall no longer be haughty in My holy mountain," and it is written, "and I will leave in your midst a poor and lowly people, and they shall take refuge in the Name of the LORD." And Rabbi Moshe of Coucy, peace be upon him, wrote in Rule 5, §64, regarding this matter, these are his words: and it does not mean literally a "poor" people, for it is written (Isaiah 60:9), "for the islands shall wait for Me, and the ships of Tarshish first, to bring your children from afar, their silver and their gold with them" — rather it means a "humble" [anav] people, and so Onkelos translated it, "a humble people." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:38: Now that we have spoken of the disgrace of pride and its punishment, we shall speak of the punishment for one who is prone to anger, for anger comes only from haughtiness of heart — for if his heart were broken and crushed, he certainly would not become angry nor respond to his own disgrace, as we say at the end of our prayer, "my God, guard my tongue from evil... and to those who curse me let my soul be silent, and let my soul be like dust to all." And in several matters the punishments for anger are equal to the punishments for pride, such as that the angry person forgets his learning, as will be explained.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:39: In Nedarim (22a) we say: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan, whoever becomes angry — all kinds of Gehinnom rule over him, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 11:10), "and remove anger from your heart and put away evil from your flesh, for youth and dark hair are vanity" — and "evil" is nothing but Gehinnom, as it is said (Proverbs 16:4), "and even the wicked for the day of evil." Moreover, intestinal ailments rule over him, as it is said (Deuteronomy 28:65), "and the LORD will give you there a trembling heart, and failing eyes, and a languishing soul" — what thing makes the eyes fail and the soul languish? Say, these are intestinal ailments. And the Rosh, of blessed memory, explained: "makes the eyes fail" — because he prolongs his illness and always hopes to be healed. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:40: And we say further there: Rabbah bar Rav Huna said, any person who becomes angry — even the Shechinah is not considered important compared to him, as it is said (Psalms 10:4), "the wicked, according to the height of his anger, does not seek [God]" etc. Rabbi Yirmeya of Difti said, he forgets his learning and increases foolishness, as it is said (Ecclesiastes 7:9), "for anger rests in the bosom of fools," and it is written (Proverbs 13:16), "but a fool spreads out folly." Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said, it is known that his sins outweigh his merits, as it is said (ibid. 29:22), "an angry man stirs up strife, and a wrathful man abounds in transgression." Thus far his words. And likewise they said in Berachot (29b): Elijah said to Rabbi Yehuda, brother of Rav Sala the Pious, "do not become enraged and you will not sin" — the reason being, "a wrathful man abounds in transgression."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:41: Further, we say in Pesachim (66b): Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said, any person who becomes angry — if he is a sage, his wisdom departs from him; if he is a prophet, his prophecy departs from him. That a sage's wisdom departs, from where do we learn this? From Moses, as it is written (Numbers 31:14), "and Moses became angry with the officers of the army" etc., and it is written (ibid. 31:21), "and Elazar the priest said to the men of the army" etc. "which the LORD commanded Moses" — implying that it had been forgotten by Moses. And that a prophet's prophecy departs from him, from where do we learn this? From Elisha, as it is written (2 Kings 3:14), "were it not that I regard the presence of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah, I would not look at you" etc. "and now bring me a musician" etc. "and the hand of the LORD came upon him" etc. [implying prophecy had left him due to his anger].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:42: Rabbi Mani bar Patish said, whoever becomes angry — even if greatness has been decreed for him from Heaven, they lower him. From where do we learn this? From Eliav, as it is said (1 Samuel 17:28), "and Eliav's anger was kindled against David, and he said, why have you come down, and with whom have you left those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your arrogance and the wickedness of your heart, for you have come down to see the battle." And when Samuel went to anoint them, of all of them it is written, "the LORD has not chosen this one," but of Eliav it is written (1 Samuel 16:7), "do not look at his appearance or his stature, for I have rejected him" — implying that he had been loved [i.e., considered] until now [and only now rejected because of his display of anger]. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:43: Further, they said in Vayikra Rabbah (13:1): Rav Huna said, in three places Moses became angry and a halakhah was hidden from him, and these are they: regarding Shabbat, regarding an onen [one whose relative died that day], and regarding metal vessels. Regarding Shabbat, as it is written (Exodus 16:20), "and some men left of it [the manna] until morning" — once he became angry, the laws of Shabbat were hidden from him; what did he tell them? (ibid. 16:25), "eat it today, for today is a Sabbath to the LORD" etc. [rather than immediately telling them of the double portion on Friday]. Regarding metal vessels, "and Moses became angry with the officers of the army" (Numbers 31:14), and once he became angry, a halakhah was hidden from him and he forgot to state the laws of [purifying] metal vessels, until Elazar stated it. Regarding an onen, from where do we learn this? (Leviticus 10:16), "and he became angry with Elazar and with Itamar" etc., and he forgot to tell them that an onen is forbidden to eat of the remaining holy offerings. Thus far his words. And they said in a Midrash regarding this matter: and if Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, of whom it is written (Numbers 12:7), "he is faithful in all My house," and who conducted himself with mercy toward Israel and gave his soul for them, saying (Exodus 32:32), "and if not, blot me" etc. — father of the sages and the prophets — when he became angry for a single moment, a halakhah was hidden from him, how much more so ordinary people.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:44: The reason for all these punishments, besides the explained reason, is that anger comes from the side of pride, and therefore what applies to the one applies closely to the other, as Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in the Zohar (portion Tetzaveh, 182a) — from there the reason will be further explained. He says there on the verse (Isaiah 2:22), "cease for yourselves from man, whose breath is in his nostrils," these are his words: and when the Holy One, blessed be He, created man, He made him in a supernal image and blew into him a holy spirit, comprising three, as we have established that he has Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, and above all is Neshamah, which is the supernal power to know and guard the commandments of the Holy One, blessed be He. And if that holy soul is brought into another service, this defiles it and it departs from the service of its Master, since these three powers are all one — Nefesh, Ruach, Neshamah join together and become one, all in the pattern of the supernal secret, corresponding to what is said (Proverbs 13:20), "he who walks with the wise shall become wise." And if we see this person in whom all these levels are — before this stands verified, to know who he is, how is it known? By approaching that person, whether to abstain from him — precisely by his anger one knows him and it becomes known who he is: if he guards that holy soul at the time of his anger and does not uproot it from its place in order for that foreign god to rest in its place — this is a proper person, this is the servant of his Master, this is a perfect man. But if that person does not guard it and uproots this supernal holiness from its place so that the Other Side rests in its place — certainly this is a person who rebels against his Master, and it is forbidden to draw near him or associate with him; this is [the meaning of] "who tears his soul in his anger" — in his anger he tears and uproots his own soul because of his rage, and installs within it a foreign god.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:45: Therefore it is written, "cease for yourselves from man, whose breath is in his nostrils," for that holy soul is torn and defiled because of his nostril [anger] — "whose breath [neshamah] is exchanged in his nostril [af]." "For wherein is he to be accounted?" — that person is accounted as idolatry, and whoever associates with him or converses with him is as though he actually associates with idolatry. Why? Because idolatry itself rests within him, and moreover, he uproots the supernal holiness from its place and installs in its place idolatry, a foreign god — just as it is written of a foreign god (Leviticus 19:4), "do not turn to idols," so it is forbidden to gaze at his face.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:46: And should you say, is this not the anger of the Sages [which is permissible]? The anger of the Sages is good on all sides, for we have learned that Torah is fire, and Torah heats it up, as it is written (Jeremiah 23:29), "are not My words like fire, says the LORD" — the anger of the Sages is over matters of Torah; the anger of the Sages is to give honor to Torah, and all of it is for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He. But if it is over other matters, this is not the service of the Holy One, blessed be He, for with all the sins a person commits, he does not become actual idolatry, and it is [only] forbidden to associate with him in this [particular sin of anger].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:47: And should you say, there was a moment when he transgressed and then returned [to calm] — it is not so, for since he has uprooted the holiness of his soul from him and from its place, and that foreign god has strengthened itself within him and does not leave him, except when the person comes entirely and uproots it forever, and afterward strives to sanctify himself and draw holiness upon himself — then, would that he be sanctified.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:48: Rabbi Yosi said to him, is he actually sanctified? He said to him, come and see: at the time he uproots the holiness of his soul and that foreign god rests in its place, the person becomes impure and is called impure, and defiles whoever comes near him, and that holiness flees from him; and once it has fled from him once, how much must the person do until it returns to its place? He said to him, if so, how many impure people become purified [after all, teshuvah is possible generally]? He said to him, this impurity is different, one that cannot be undone [easily] — but this differs from everything: it defiles the body within and without, and the soul, and defiles everything, whereas other impurity in the world affects only the body outwardly alone. Therefore, "cease for yourselves from man, whose breath is in his nostril," for he has exchanged the holiness of his Master because of his nostril [anger], and this is the impurity that defiles everything; "for wherein is he to be accounted" — he is certainly accounted as idolatry.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:49: Come and see: this anger is idolatry, the Other Side, as I have said, and a person must guard himself from it and separate himself from it. Therefore it is written (Exodus 34:17), "you shall not make molten gods for yourself" — "for yourself," to harm yourself — and it is written after it (ibid. 23:18), "you shall keep the feast of matzot" — this is the side of holiness that a person must guard, and not exchange it for the Other Side; and if he exchanges it, he becomes impure and defiles whoever comes near him. "You shall keep the feast of matzot" — this is a place called "guard" [shamor], and therefore it is written, "you shall keep the feast of matzot." Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:50: When a person considers what Rashbi, peace be upon him, explained in this statement — that the angry person uproots all the holiness within him, which is Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, and because these three are a single bond, the verse calls them collectively "his soul," "tears his soul" etc. — this is what is meant by "these three powers are all one." Rashbi, peace be upon him, informs us in this statement of the greatness of the punishment, so that we should not say that the blemish is only in the Nefesh alone but not in the rest — for this is not so, but all the holiness within him departs, since once the kelipah dwells in him, holiness flees, for he brings in and installs the maidservant in the place of her mistress — since this is actual idolatry, resembling the sin of idolatry that Israel committed when they brought an idol into the Sanctuary, causing the Shechinah to flee from there, as is known.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:51: Therefore, since a foreign god, which is idolatry, dwells within him, defiling his body and soul in such a way, it is just that he forget his learning, for forgetfulness is the kelipah, as it says (Genesis 40:23), "and the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:52: And the Shechinah is not considered important compared to him, as is explained at the end of this statement regarding "you shall keep the feast of matzot — this is the side of holiness." The matter is that "God has made the one alongside the other" (Ecclesiastes 7:14) — just as the Shechinah is the totality of all the supernal attributes, and through her the providence and dominion of the Cause of all Causes are made visible, as explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 1, so too the foreign god, which is her counterpart, has all the powers of impurity included within it, and it denies providence, as we explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 8. Therefore it says, "all kinds of Gehinnom," for all are drawn from this kelipah, and all the other punishments are explained by this.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:53: Now, the Shechinah rests only upon a broken and crushed heart, and since he is angry, his heart becomes proud within him, and immediately a foreign god rests upon him, this being the totality of impurity; therefore it says it is forbidden to associate with him, since idolatrous worship is called "sacrifices of the dead," and an idolatrous offering defiles either by carrying it or under the same roof [ohel], according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira, as they said in tractate Chullin, chapter 1 (13a) regarding a gentile's slaughter — it is [considered] carrion and defiles by carrying — they said there, it was taught, Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says, from where do we learn that an idolatrous offering defiles under the same roof? As it is said (Psalms 106:28), "and they attached themselves to Baal Peor and ate sacrifices of the dead" — just as a corpse defiles under the same roof, so an idolatrous offering defiles under the same roof. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:54: I heard from the mouth of Rabbi Yitzchak Ashkenazi, peace be upon him, that "tears his soul" means that he makes it a treifah [an animal with a fatal wound, unfit to eat]. And it is possible to be precise about this interpretation in the wording of the Zohar, which says that holy soul "is torn and defiled because of his anger" — and its saying "defiled" [makes sense] since it is a treifah, and a treifah is called dead, for a treifah does not live twelve months (Chullin 57b), and certainly defiles. Likewise the angry person: since his holy soul was dwelling in his heart, and once he brings in the kelipah, an adhesion attaches itself to it and defiles the soul. And so it says further below, "and defiles the soul and everything." And this does not resemble an animal that is a treifah, which does not defile if it was slaughtered with a kosher knife, but here he makes it carrion, since he slaughters the soul with a blemished knife, which is Samael, Sam El Zar [poison, god, stranger].
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:55: It is likewise possible to be precise about this interpretation in the wording of the Zohar, which says, this is called "tearing his soul in his anger," he tears and uproots his soul because of his rage, and it says "uproots" — this being the "uprooting of the signs," one of the five things that invalidate slaughter, making it carrion and defiling by carrying; and just as the uprooting of the signs is the uprooting of the matter contrary to the accepted order, being outside the natural process, so with the angry person: the essential holiness has a nature to dwell in a person, for that is why he was created, and he, against its will, uproots it from its place. We find, then, two interpretations in the word "tearing," and both are true.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:56: Along these lines we find that an angry person who is a Kohen defiles himself with the impurity of a corpse, since all souls are from the side of Abraham, called "Kohen," as explained in portion Mishpatim (95a), that the daughter of a Kohen is the daughter of Abraham; and since he becomes angry, he kills his soul, and the dead defile — thus a Kohen defiles himself with the impurity of a corpse.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:57: Further, we find a warning against the angry person written in the verse (Psalms 81:10), "there shall be no foreign god within you" etc., which is explained in tractate Shabbat (105b): Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar in the name of Rabbi Chalafta ben Agra, who said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri: whoever tears his garments in his rage, or breaks vessels in his rage, or scatters his money in his rage, should be in your eyes like one who worships idols, for such is the craft of the evil inclination: today it tells him do this, and tomorrow it tells him do that, and the next day it tells him, go worship idols, and he goes and worships. And Rabbi Yochanan said, what is the verse? "There shall be no foreign god within you" — which is the foreign god that is in a person's own body? This is the evil inclination. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:58: And in the Zohar (portion Pekudei, 263b), in the first chamber of the chambers of impurity, they said, these are their words: and above these is an appointed one named Sifsarita, and several guardians of the laws [of impurity], and this appointed one over them takes these evil words, and likewise takes all these that a person casts with his hands when rage rests upon him — for then this appointed one, Sifsarita, takes this word that the person casts in his rage, and ascends and says, "this is the offering of so-and-so, offered to our side" — for every side of tranquility is from the side of the right and from the side of faith, and every side of rage is from the evil Other Side, the impure side. Therefore whoever casts something from his hand in rage — all these take up that word that was cast and bring it up above and it is brought near to that side, and they say, this is the offering of so-and-so; and a herald calls out in all those firmaments and says, woe to so-and-so who has strayed after a foreign god and worships another god; and the herald calls out a second time and says (Hosea 6:12 [actually 7:13]), "woe to them, for they have strayed from Me" etc. Fortunate is the person who guards his ways and does not stray to the right or to the left, and does not fall into a deep pit from which he cannot ascend. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:59: Through this statement, Rashbi's statement that we copied above, "you shall keep the feast of matzot — this is the side of holiness," is further explained, mentioning in it the term "guarding" [shemirah] as explained above. And she is the Shechinah, called "matzah," who has no admixture of chametz, which are the kelipot, and is called "the feast of matzot" in the aspect of the right, which is Abraham, "Pesach" corresponds to the right arm (Zohar, portion Tetzeh, 282b); and therefore Rashbi says, "every side of tranquility is from the side of the right and from the side of faith" — this being the secret of the profession of Israel, all bound to the Shechinah, as explained in the Gate of Awe, ch. 1 — and from the side of the right, as explained, one who is not angry does not include himself in the side of judgment; and the angry person arouses the bile [marah], which is the root of judgment, and therefore all kinds of Gehinnom rule over him, since he arouses judgment from its root, as it is written (Daniel 7:10), "a river of fire flowed and issued forth before Him," and in the nose of Ze'ir [Anpin] there is the root of judgment, as it is written (Deuteronomy 32:22), "for a fire is kindled in My nostril and burns to the depths of Sheol" — and the place where the river of fire pours out is in Gehinnom, resting upon the heads of the wicked, as explained in the Gate of Awe, chapter 13. Therefore they said in Tikkunim (85a) that the angry person is as though he had kindled the fire of Gehinnom. These are his words, in Tikkun 48: fortunate is one who guards a fitting dwelling for the Shabbat, which is the heart, so that neither the sorrow of the spleen nor the anger of the bile, which is the fire of Gehinnom, be brought near there — of this it is said (Exodus 35:3), "you shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the Sabbath day," and this is certainly so, for whoever becomes angry is as though he kindles the fire of Gehinnom. Thus far his words. And in the Ra'aya Meheimna (beginning of 234b) they explain this matter further; see there.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:60: When we are precise about the statement that says, "and this appointed one over them takes these evil words, and likewise takes" etc., there are two things: "evil words" are the bad things said in anger that a person suddenly casts from his mouth — this appointed one is appointed only over anger, since over all disgraceful speech another appointed one is already mentioned above, and over evil speech [lashon hara] another is mentioned further below in Chamber 3, etc. Likewise he is appointed over things thrown from a person's hand, and this is meant by "and likewise takes" — for if these are related matters, it is fitting to say "and likewise takes," so it seems to me. We find, then, that the blemish of anger is in the first chamber of the kelipah, since it blemishes the Mistress and enthrones the maidservant, and she will take her revenge upon him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:61: It is explained in the Zohar (portion Tazria, 43a) that once a person casts something from his hand in anger, from that moment he is handed over to the kelipah and there is no blessing in the work of his hands. These are his words: come and see, it is forbidden for a person to throw the vessels of his house and hand them over to the Other Side unnecessarily, or another similar thing, for several guardians of the laws [of impurity] are ready to receive that thing, and from that moment blessing does not rest upon him, for it is from the Other Side; and all the more so one who assigns his own supernal goodness to another, to the Other Side, since it comes from that which he assigned it to — and when a person's days draw near for him to depart this world, that supernal image given to him, that spirit that had attached itself to him every day, comes and takes it and is repaired within it and departs, and never returns to that person again; then he knows that he has been rejected from everything. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 2:62: Now that we have spoken of the punishments for pride and anger, we shall come to explain in a separate chapter what matters a person should consider in his mind so as not to come to anger, and not respond to his own disgrace:
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:1: The matters a person should take to heart in order not to become angry are these. First, what our Sages of blessed memory said explicitly (Pesachim 113b), and likewise in Chupat Eliyahu (Gate of the Three): three does the Holy One, blessed be He, love — one who does not become angry, one who does not become drunk, and one who does not insist on his own way [ma'amid al middotav]. Thus far his words. The reason the Holy One, blessed be He, loves them is that these three are a chariot for Chesed, called Love, as it is written (Jeremiah 31:3), "and with everlasting love I have loved you; therefore I have drawn you with kindness."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:2: One who does not become angry — it has already been explained above that the angry person arouses the power of the bile, which is the root of judgment, and thus becomes distant from Chesed. Likewise one who becomes drunk is from the side of judgment, from the side of harsh wine, which does not arouse love; and one who does not become drunk is found not to enjoy wine, which is judgment, but rather what is close to arousing the love of Chesed, and therefore the Holy One, blessed be He, loves him. Likewise one who does not insist on his own way is bound to Chesed, which does good both to the good and to the bad, for the Holy One, blessed be He, from the side of Chesed, does not repay a person according to his deeds, as it is written (Psalms 103:8), "merciful and gracious is the LORD, slow to anger and abundant in kindness; He will not always strive, nor keep His anger forever; He has not dealt with us according to our sins" etc. — but one who insists on his own way, deserving to be repaid measure for measure, is bound to the side of judgment, which is exacting in giving to a man according to his ways and the fruit of his deeds. And these three are three lines in order, from the side of prevailing Chesed.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:3: The merits that come to one who overlooks his own honor [ma'avir al middotav] are these: first, that he lengthens his days in this world, and further, that his transgressions are overlooked, as we learn in tractate Megillah (28a): Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Nechunya the Great, through what did you lengthen your days? He said to him, in all my days I never accepted gifts, and I never insisted on my own way, and I was generous with my money. As with Rabbi Elazar: when they would send him gifts from the house of the Nasi, he would not accept them; when they would invite him, he would not go, saying to them, it would not be good for you if I should live [since accepting gifts corrupts judgment], for it is written (Proverbs 15:27), "and he who hates gifts shall live." Rabbi Zeira: when they would send to him from the house of the Nasi, he would not take it; when they would invite him, he would go, saying, it is an honor for them that I am honored by them [not accepting undue favors]. "And I never insisted on my own way" — for Rava said, whoever overlooks his own honor has all his own transgressions overlooked, as it is said, "forgiving iniquity and overlooking transgression" — for whom does He forgive iniquity? For one who overlooks transgression [against himself]. Thus far his words. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained in tractate Rosh Hashanah (17a) regarding this statement: "one who overlooks his own way" is one who is not exacting in measuring measure for measure against those who trouble him, but sets aside his [claim to his] own way and moves on — like "we do not disturb the fulfillment of mitzvot," "we do not disturb foods" — he sets them aside and moves on. "They overlook all his transgressions" — the attribute of judgment is not exacting after them, but sets them aside and moves on.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:4: Further, they said in Sanhedrin (92a), these are their words: and Rabbi Elazar said, always be among the "receivers" and thereby endure — meaning, be lowly and you will live; and certainly one who is lowly is humble and does not insist on his own way.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:5: Further, a third merit is that he is saved from an unnatural death, as they said in the Zohar (portion Miketz, 201b) about a certain man who had this merit and was saved from an unnatural death. These are his words: Rabbi Abba was sitting at the gate of the entrance to Lod, and he saw a certain man coming and sitting on a mound of overhanging earth, weary from the road, and he sat and fell asleep there. Meanwhile he saw a snake coming toward him; a mongoose came out and killed the snake. When that man awoke, he saw that snake before him, dead, and the man stood up and that mound fell into the depth beneath him and he was saved. Rabbi Abba came to him and said, tell me your deeds, for the Holy One, blessed be He, has performed for you these two miracles — they are not for nothing. That man said to him, in all my days no wicked person has ever completed [an act against me] in the world without my being reconciled with him and forgiving him; moreover, if I was not able to be reconciled with him, I would not go up to my bed until I had forgiven him and all those who trouble me, and I never took to heart, day to day, the evil that was done to me — and it is not enough for me [merely to forgive], but from that day on I strive to do good with them. Rabbi Abba wept and said, this man's deeds are greater than Joseph's — Joseph's [brothers] were certainly his brothers and he should have had mercy on them, but what this man does is greater than Joseph, and it is fitting that the Holy One, blessed be He, perform miracle upon miracle for him. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:6: I found this quality — which was found in this pious man — written of a certain Rav, counted among ten qualities he possessed, one of them being that whoever provoked him, he would go and appease him.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:7: So too Rabbeinu Yonah, peace be upon him, wrote in Sefer HaYirah, these are his words: be reconciled to your brother and your fellow, and do not lie down at night with a quarrel between you and another person, but go and reconcile with him until he is appeased; and even if he sinned against you, seek reconciliation from him, and do not say, he sinned against me, it is up to him to appease me — subdue your inclination and go to him, so that your heart not become proud and you become detestable before the Creator, as it is said (Proverbs 16:5), "an abomination to the LORD is every proud heart."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:8: Further, a fourth merit is that his judgment decree is torn up and life is added to him — for if he becomes ill and inclines toward death, and they examine his deeds and find him worthy of this merit, he is saved from death to life. And so they said in tractate Rosh Hashanah (17a), these are their words: Rav Huna the son of Rav Yehoshua became ill; Rav Pappa came to visit him and saw that the world was slipping away from him [i.e., he was dying]. He said to them, prepare his shrouds. In the end he recovered. Rav Pappa was ashamed to see him. He [Rav Huna] said to him, what did you see [that made you think I would die]? He said, so it was [decreed]. He said to them, the Holy One, blessed be He, said, since he does not insist on his own way, do not insist [with judgment] against him, as it is said (Micah 7:18), "forgiving iniquity and overlooking transgression" — for whom does He forgive iniquity? For one who overlooks transgression [against himself] — "for the remnant of His inheritance." Rabbi Acha bar Chanina said, [this is like] honey with a thorn in it — "for the remnant of His inheritance," and not for the whole of His inheritance — for one who makes himself like ownerless property [i.e., humbly overlooked, not insisting on rights]. Thus far his words. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "prepare his shrouds" — prepare provisions for his journey, meaning the provision of the dead, shrouds. "He recovered" — was healed. "So it was" — death had been decreed upon me. "Does not insist on his own way" — does not insist on his own way. "Do not insist [with judgment] against him" — do not be exacting after him. "Honey with a thorn in it" — meaning, there is a comforting word here, but there is a harsh element within it that does not apply equally to all. Thus far his words. And in Midrash Ruth (Zohar Chadash) they brought a similar story about Rabbi Karospedai, who became ill and inclined toward death and was taken up to that world, and it happened, etc.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:9: In Chupat Eliyahu they brought a story close to this wording, on the same matter, regarding the statement we copied at the beginning of the chapter — "three does the Holy One, blessed be He, love" etc. These are his words: Rav Huna, the son of Rav Yehoshua, became ill and was taken to that world for several nights and days. When he returned, they said to him, Rabbi, with what were you released? He said to them, my sons, fortunate is one who does not insist on his own way. I swear, companies of ministering angels came and pleaded merit for me, but it was not accepted from them, until an angel came and said, for whom are you pleading merit — is it not for this one who never insisted on his own way? Immediately they released me from death to life.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:10: Further there, near this passage, they brought a wondrous story about one who does not insist on his own way. These are his words: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak had a mound of earth in his vineyard, and he brought laborers there to dig up the mound, and they dug it all that day. On the second day, as they were digging, a man leaped out from within his house and sat on the mound and began to sway and call out — and what was he calling? "Perhaps the resurrection of the dead has arrived, perhaps the resurrection of the dead has arrived!" The laborers ran and told Rav Nachman. He came and found him. He said to him, who are you? He said to him, I am dead — perhaps the time of the resurrection of the dead has arrived. He said to him, what is your business on this mound? He said to him, did I not tell you I am dead? He said to him, does a dead man not rot? He said to him, did they not bring you into the house of study and read to you the book of Proverbs? Did Solomon not say (Proverbs 14:30), "and envy is the rot of the bones"? In all my days I never insisted on my own way, and I never held envy of my fellow in my heart, and I never spoke idly, neither in the study hall nor in the synagogue, but gave my heart and eyes only to words of Torah, to fulfill what is said (ibid. 1:33), "and whoever listens to me shall dwell securely." Rav Nachman said to him, I will build for you a chamber [as a monument]. He said to him, do nothing for me, and do not move me from this place, for I was buried here with permission — rather, return the earth that was taken from over me to its place. And Rav Nachman was frightened and grieved all that day, saying, woe is me, perhaps I have disturbed that dead man. Immediately he saw in a dream that he was sitting in a myrtle-branch sukkah. He immediately gave praise and thanks before the Holy One, blessed be He, and read this verse (Proverbs 8:34), "fortunate is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors." May the name of the King of kings of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He, be praised, for He does not withhold the reward of any creature — and if this man, whose merit was only silence and not insisting on his own way, was repaid thus by the Holy One, blessed be He, how much more so will the Holy One, blessed be He, repay doubled and redoubled reward to one who accustoms himself to the study of Torah, raises his children to the study of Torah, and walks in service and lowliness of spirit. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:11: Further, a sixth merit is that the prayer of one who overlooks his own way is heard, as is proven in Ta'anit (25b). It says there: a story of Rabbi Eliezer, who went down before the Ark and said twenty-four benedictions, and was not answered; Rabbi Akiva went down and said "Avinu Malkeinu" and was answered. A heavenly voice went out and said, it is not that this one is greater than that one, but that this one overlooks his own way, and that one does not overlook his own way. Thus far his words.
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:12: Further, a seventh merit is that the world is sustained through it, as they explained in tractate Chullin, end of chapter 6 (89a): Rabbi Ila'i said, the world is sustained only through one who restrains his mouth at a time of strife, as it is said (Job 26:7), "He hangs the earth upon nothing [belimah]." Rabbi Abahu said, [through one] who makes himself as though he were nothing, as it is said (Deuteronomy 33:27), "and underneath are the everlasting arms." Thus far his words. And Rashi, of blessed memory, explained: "restrains" — closes his mouth; "underneath" — one who is trampled underneath everything, he is the "arms of the world."
Reshit Chokhmah, Gate of Humility 3:13: Further, an eighth and ninth merit: that he merits Torah, and that Elijah reveals himself to him — for Torah is explained only to one who is not irritable, and Elijah reveals himself only to one who is not irritable, as is explained in tractate Kallah Rabbati, chapter "Be Careful in Judging Your Words" (ch. 5), these are his words: Father Elijah, of blessed memory, said, Torah is explained only to one who is not irritable; I too reveal myself only to one who is not irritable. Fortunate is one who meets him, and one who sits with him, for it is guaranteed to him that he is a son of the World to Come. Thus far his words.
